full_judgment:
2. The facts, relevant for disposal of this civil appeal, in short, are that the plaintiffs [hereinafter referred to as the appellants] instituted Title Suit No.43 of 1993 in the Court Assistant Judge, Amtoli, Borguna for declaration of the title and recovery of khas possession stating, inter alia, that the suit land originally belonged to one Abdus Sattar and others. The suit land was sold in auction and the same was purchased by plaintiff No.3 on 30.06.1986 who sold out 6 decimals of land to plaintiff No.1 on 14.02.1987 by registered deed. Plaintiff Nos.1 and 3 have been possessing the same by mutating their names in the khatian and paying rent to the Government. Plaintiff No.2 took settlement of 10 decimals of land from plot Nos.921 and 934 recorded in khas khatian No.1 registered by kabuliat dated 12.11.1986 from the Government. In this way, the plaintiffs became the owners of 22 decimals of land. On the 11th day of Falgoon, 1396 B.S. defendant No.1 dispossessed the plaintiffs from the suit land. The plaintiffs requested defendant No.1 to vacate the land, but he did not pay any heed. Hence, the plaintiffs instituted the suit. 

 3. Defendant No.1 contested the suit by filing written statement denying the material allegation contending, inter alia, that the suit land appertaining to PS Khatian No.4 of Mouza-Amtoli originally belonged to one Zaminder Zadunath Saha Chowdhury and others who settled 1.81 acres of land to their tenants and kept 1.47 acres of land in their khas possession. One Sukh Lai Saha and others were the owners of the land of PS Khatin No.7 and they settled 2.93 acres of land to the tenants and kept 2.59 acres of land in their khas possession. Zadunath Saha and others through their Naeb Shailendra Nath Sahaettled the land to one Tazem Ali Howlader, the predecessor of defendant No.l. Shailendra Nath executed a salami receipt on 5 Baishakh, 1359 BS on behalf of the Zamindars receiving taka 100 as salami from Tazem Ali Howladar. Tazem All Howlader erected dwelling homestead and planted trees etc in the said land. In this way, his father had been a tenant under the Zamindar with regard to 66 decimals of land including the disputed land and thereafter, on 15.01.1960 his father orally gifted him the disputed land by delivering possession. Defendant No.1 has been possessing the disputed land since 1960. During revisional survey 1.87 acres of land of PS khatian Nos.4, 7, and 12 including the 66 decimals of land which were given pattan to his father Tazem Ali Howladar was wrongly recorded in Hal Plot No.934 of Khatian No.1 in the name of Government. The plaintiffs have had no right, title, interest and possession in the suit land. 

 9. Ms. Sayeda Nasrin, learned Advocate, appearing for the appellant, submits that the suit land was recorded in the name of the Government under khas khatian No.1 during SA operation and it vested in the Government and thereafter, the Government settled the suit land in favour of plaintiff Nos.1 and 2 by registered kabuliat vide Certificate Case No.827 of 1980-81 and Lease Case No.02 of AM-1985-86 and thereafter, they mutated their names and paid rent to the Government for the suit land. She further submits that the appellant got settlement of the suit land from the Government by registered kabuliat and got physical possession from the Government and this fact was proved by the plaintiffs by producing both documentary and oral evidence. She further submits that both the Courts below con-currently found the title and possession of the plaintiffs in the suit land pursuant to the settlement case and certificate case and delivery of possession was given by the Government and the concurrent findings of fact as arrived at by both the Courts below are based on material evidence on record. It is finally submitted that there was no misreading or non-consideration of the material evidence on record and the concurrent findings of fact of both the Courts below cannot be interfered by the High Court Division in revisional jurisdiction. 

 10. Per contra, Mr. Shahidul Islam, learned Advocate, appearing on behalf of respondent No.1, contends that the plaintiff-appellant totally failed to prove his title and possession in the suit land within 12 years of institution of the suit. He further contends that the fact of settlement allegedly granted by the Additional Deputy Commissioner, Barguna in favour of the plaintiffs father vide exhibit-2[Certified copy of Kabuliat dated 12.11.1986] having not proved and allegedly having granted settlement for an unspecified area of .07 decimals out of 1.87 acres of land of Plot No.934, the suit for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession was not tenable in Law. He adds that exhibit-3[Certified copy of Boinama of Certificate Case No.827 of 1980-81 and dakhalnama] cannot be construed to be a document of handing over possession in favour of the plaintiff upon an unspecified 07 decimals of land out of 1.87 acres of land when the defendants' two storied dwelling house has been constructed upon a part of Plot No.934. He further contends that Pw-1, in his cross-examination, deposed that 'আমাদের settlement দেয়ার অর্থ দখল দেয়া। যে তারেখেই settlement দেয়া সেই তারিখেই Surveyor আমাদের মেপে জমি বুঝিয়ে দিয়ে আসে।' It is an evidence on oath which clearly disclosed that the plaintiffs have instituted the suit for recovery of khas possession followed by dispossession being out of possession and was not maintainable. He further contends that the evidence adduced by Dw-1 proved it beyond doubt that the defendant has been possessing his homestead, constructed upon a part of the suit plot continuously since 1960. He finally contends that there is no evidence in support of handing over possession in favour of the plaintiffs in the suit land within period from 30.06.1986 to 14.02.1987 and the settlement from the Government dated 12.11.1986 having not proved, the evidence on record proved it beyond doubt that the plaintiffs instituted the suit being out of possession. 

 12. The claim of the plaintiff-appellants is that they are the owners of the land by Nilam purchase and by purchasing with consideration money vide registered kabala and kabuliyat from the owners of the land, i.e. from the Government as khas land lease and they possessed the land. Devastating Tornedo and flood washed away their house, so the land remained vacant. When WAPDA cut mud from there, a ditch was made therein where the defendant erected houses illegally, forcibly dispossessing the plaintiffs from 'Ka' scheduled land on 11 Falgoon, 1396 BS. A local salish was held wherein the defendants admitted that they would hand over possession. The land in question has properly been recorded in the name of the plaintiffs when the defendant has failed to mutate his name and his rather also failed to mutate his name in the disputed khatian. The plaintiffs claimed that they have been able to prove their right, title and interest in the suit land by producing parchas, boinama, dakhalnama, kabuliyat, rent receipts which are public documents. In support of their contention, they cited the cases: Brahma Nand Puri-Vs-Neki Puri, reported in AIR1965SC1506 and Vijay Pullarwar-Vs-Shri Hanuman Deostan, (2019)11SCC718. 

 16. On perusal of the documents on record, it appears that 12 decimals of land of Plot No.935 of SA Khatian No.789 under Amtalimouza belong to Abdus Sattar, Birendra Bijoy Das and others. The aforesaid land was auctioned on 30.06.1986 and plaintiff No. 3 purchased the same. On 14.02.1987, plaintiff No.3 by a registered deed of sale transferred six decimals of land of Plot No.935 to plain-tiff No. l. Plaintiff Nos.3 and 1 mutated their names. Bijendra Bijoy Das, father of plaintiff No.3 achieved pattan of 3 decimals of land of Plot No.921 and 7 decimals of land of Plot No.934 in total 10 decimals of land from khas khatian No.1 of the Government through Settlement Case No.2(Am) of 1985-86. A Kabuliyat deed was registered on 12.11.1986 after having salami of taka 1750 and a new khatian No. 1326 was created in the name of Birendra Bijoy Das. The plaintiffs exhibited original parcha of SA khatian No.1326, certified copy of Kabuliyat dated 12.1.1.1986, the boinama and dakhalnama of certificate case No. 827(Am) of 1980-81, DCR of payment of salami taka 1.750 dated 10.11.1986, certified copy of SA Khatian No.789 and certified copies of order sheet of Settlement Case No.2(Am)/ 85-86.In the instant suit, the plaintiffs have produced documentary evidence, most of which are public in nature, regarding their title to the suit land. They also produced documentary evidence dhakhalnama and rent receipts in support of their possession to the suit land before dispossession. Simultaneously, they produced oral evidence in support of their title and possession followed by dispossession from the suit land. It appears that Pw-1 consistently deposed in support of the plaint that they took possession of the suit land in accordance with certificate case, boinama, dakhalnama, sale deed, and kabuliyat but on 23'02/1990 corresponding to 11 Falgoon, 1396 B.E. Defendant No.1 dispossessed them from the suit lard by force. Pw-1 did not depose contrary to his statement during cross-examination. Pw-2 and Pw-3 duly corroborated the testimony of Pw-1 regarding the plaintiffs' title and possession (before dispossession) to the suit land. It appears that Pw-2 materially corroborated the testimony of Pw-1 to the effect that on 11 Falgoon, 1396 B.S. defendant No.1 dispossessed the plaintiffs from the suit land. Likewise, Pw-3 substantially corroborated the testimony of Pw-1 that during 1396 B.S. defendant no 1 dispossessed the plaintiffs from the suit land. It appears that the plaintiffs have primarily been able to prove their title and possession (before dispossession) to the suit land and they have discharged their initial burden of proof. Now it is the turn of defendant No.1 to discharge his onus of proof. In terms of Section 102 of the Evidence act, 1872, the initial onus to prove its claim is always on the plaintiff and if he discharges that onus and makes out a case which entitles him to a relief, the onus shifts to the defendant to prove these circumstances, if any, which would disentitle the plaintiff to the same [Bharat Alumnium Co.-V- Maharashtra Alumnium Co., 2009 DLT 489]. In a suit for possession based on title once the plaintiff has been able to create a high degree of probability so as to shift the onus on the defendant, it is for the defendant to discharge his onus and in the absence thereof, the burden of proof lying on the plaintiff shall be held to have been discharged so as to amount to proof of the plaintiffs title [R. V. E. Venkatachala Gounder -V- Arulmigu Viswesaraswaini and V. P. Temple, AIR 2003 SC 4548]. Let us have an overview of the defendant's case to see defendant No.1 has been able to discharge his onus of proof.
